summary: Examines a synchronization problem in SMTP that can cause a message to be delivered more than once, and suggests a way to avoid it. Some familiarity with the SMTP specification in RFC 821 is required.

eli5.summary: If a delivery person doesn't hear that the package arrived, they may bring a second copy. This memo shows how mail can end up sent twice and how to stop it.

questions: why do duplicate emails happen with smtp
how to avoid duplicate message delivery in smtp
how to prevent duplicate mail delivery
subtitle: Why SMTP can deliver the same message twice and how to prevent it.

tldr.problem: SMTP has a synchronization gap: after the receiving mailer decides to accept a message but before the sending mailer gets confirmation, a network failure causes both to believe they are responsible for delivery, resulting in duplicates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the critical moment: the sending mailer sends a final dot to mark the end of the message and waits for a 250 reply. If the connection breaks during this window, the sender times out and resends, not knowing the receiver already accepted it.
tldr.outcome: The solution is simple: receiving mailers should send the 250 reply as soon as the message is safely queued to disk, without waiting for further processing. Sending mailers should use longer timeouts (5 to 10 minutes) to accommodate legitimate processing delays.

today: RFC 1047 documents a widespread problem in 1988 SMTP implementations. Modern SMTP practice broadly follows the RFC's guidance: receivers acknowledge as soon as possible, and senders use reasonable timeouts. However, strict compliance varies, and duplicate messages remain a concern in email systems for other reasons (forwarding loops, retransmission logic bugs).

sections.title: The Duplicate Message Problem
sections.content:
Mail administrators were often asked to investigate why a single message had been delivered multiple times to its recipients. Investigation revealed a pattern: many duplicates were caused by a synchronization problem in SMTP itself, not mail loops or retransmission queues gone haywire.

The CSNET Coordination and Information Center (CIC) studied this extensively and found that the synchronization gap at the end of message delivery was the second leading cause of duplicate messages on the Internet (after mail loops). This seemed counterintuitive because the gap appeared brief, but in practice it was often long enough for timeouts or network failures.
sections.eli5: When you put a letter in the mail, there's a moment between when the post office takes it and when you know for sure they took it. If you assume they didn't and send another copy, the recipient gets two.

sections.title: The Critical Moment
sections.content:
In SMTP, the sender ends the message by transmitting a line containing only a single dot (period). The receiver is then expected to perform final processing and send either a 250 reply (success) or an error code. SMTP defines this as the boundary: until the receiver sends the 250, the sender must assume delivery failed.

But here is the problem: the receiver may have already written the message to disk and decided to accept it, yet the 250 reply has not been sent. If the network link breaks at this exact moment, the sender will timeout and resend the message, not knowing it was already accepted. Both mailers now have the message queued for delivery.
sections.eli5: The package is on the shelf, but you haven't heard 'received'. You knock again, nobody answers, so you leave another copy.

sections.title: Minimizing the Gap
sections.content:
The RFC cites RFC 821, which states that receiving mailers should accept messages and queue them for processing, acknowledging errors later in separate messages if needed. This allows mailers to send the 250 reply as soon as the message is on disk (non-volatile storage), without waiting for delivery to local users, mailing list expansion, or other intensive processing.

Additionally, sending mailers should use longer timeouts for the final dot reply. Many mailers use 1 to 2 minutes, which is too short given modern network latencies and legitimate processing delays. A timeout of at least 5 minutes, and preferably 10 minutes, is recommended to avoid spurious retransmissions.
sections.eli5: The post office should say 'got it' immediately after filing it away, not after reading it, sorting it, and delivering it. And you should wait a full 10 minutes before assuming they didn't get it.

references.text: Postel, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 821, August 1982.
